title: Young women striving in Agriculture & Business
summary: A profile of Salome Isaack’s journey from household dependence to agroecology, poultry and small-business entrepreneurship in Nzega District.

author.name: Joseph Masonda
author.role: Communications Officer | Digital Marketer | Website Designer | Content Creator | AI Enthusiast | Framer Developer | Writer

content.text: In Tanzania, many people live below the poverty line, with women especially exposed to economic hardship. Subsistence agriculture accounts for a large share of women’s jobs, yet the sector’s contribution to national income does not match the scale of employment. The feminisation of poverty is a real challenge, particularly in agriculture.

At the same time, women are active in micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), where they can achieve progress when they have access to finance and capacity-building support to professionalise and develop their activities.
There was therefore a need to provide young women with vocational training and support to create micro and small businesses around agroecology.

Salome Isaack is a young woman from Iyombo Village in Nzega District, Tabora Region, who is passionate about agriculture and entrepreneurship. She had spent years as a housewife, doing household work and depending on her husband for money to buy small household items. Her ambition to start a business grew as the challenges increased.

Msichana Initiative, Sustainable Agriculture Tanzania (SAT) and Practical Permaculture Institute of Zanzibar (PPIZ), with financial support from the French Embassy, developed a project titled Girls Empowerment through Agroecology and Permaculture (GAPE). When facilitators came to Nzega District, Salome saw an opportunity to learn about organic agriculture and business.

She joined the Umoja Ni Nguvu group with other young women in her village. Using lessons from SAT’s organic agriculture training, she started a small garden near her home. She planted spinach and began harvesting after seven weeks, earning TZS 8,000. She used the income to begin a poultry business by buying three chickens.
She applied what she learned about poultry feeding, better shelters, use of biopesticides and commercial breeding.

Our facilitators taught us different methods of feeding chickens, vaccination of chickens and other ways to prevent diseases in chickens, and I used those methods properly where so far I see the results are good.

Salome expanded to 30 chickens and set a goal to grow the poultry business until she could support herself financially. In the 2021 season, she also cultivated sunflower and maize, harvesting three bags of maize and three bags of sunflower in her first season. The results changed her perspective about agriculture.

Agriculture is not only about food or income. It also plays a role in protecting the environment. Organic agriculture supports environmental care and biodiversity, particularly as chemical pesticides can damage ecological systems.

Through training, Salome gained a stronger appreciation for environmental protection and healthy food for her family and future generations. She planted medicinal plants such as neem trees and wild plantains, which can be used in remedies for animal and crop illnesses. She also dug a water pond to irrigate crops and used irrigation to grow maize and beans.

Salome wanted to establish a business because extra income could improve her family’s standard of living and help meet basic needs. Success with seasonal crops and organic agriculture became a potential source of capital for her business ambitions.

At 25, Salome and four friends formed a unity group and started a pumpkin business. For TZS 12,000, they hired a gourd tree from an Iyombo villager, harvested the pumpkins, added value and sold them wholesale and retail. The business had raised TZS 40,000.

Salome used profits from the pumpkin business to operate a clothing and fabric business. She buys clothes in Nzega town and resells them at a higher price. She also redesigns some fabrics into children’s clothing and sells them in neighbouring villages.

Despite these achievements, Salome still faces challenges, including unreliable water for irrigation and limited transport to reach other villages. Yet she remains committed to farming and business, making her an inspiring example of perseverance and entrepreneurship.
